title: LSU Union Art Gallery
subtitle: Building Community Through Art, 1964–2016
credit: Flyers, photographs and negatives from the records of the LSU Union Art Gallery, LSU Libraries Special Collections.
cover_alt: Noon in My Garden, a painting by Janice Sachse

pages.title: Introduction
pages.lead_alt: Noon in My Garden, a painting by Janice Sachse
pages.lead_caption: Janice Sachse, Noon in My Garden, from the gallery’s retrospective of her work

blocks.body:
When you think of the art world at LSU, you probably think first of the Allen Hall murals and of LSU’s many locations of galleries and museums, past and present. While the Allen Hall murals are well known and likely the most viewed part of LSU art history due to their central location, another truly influential venue for art is The Union Art Gallery. It served as an important venue for bringing the art world to LSU and exploring Louisiana culture while occupying a space frequently passed by students, making it accessible to the entire student body.

LSU’s art galleries today are mainly located either in art buildings like Barnes Ogden or downtown and off-campus at venues like the Glassell Gallery and the LSU Museum of Art (MOA). The Union Art Gallery operated differently; many of its events were not only interdisciplinary and designed to appeal to a large group of students but also were on campus and easily accessible for viewing.

LSU Special Collections in Hill Memorial Library holds records of the Union Art Gallery containing flyers from various exhibitions and photos or negatives of displayed works. It also houses the records of influential figures who gave talks in conjunction with these shows, revealing the scale of artistic and educational events organized for the LSU and Baton Rouge community.

The Union Art Gallery operated with its committee from 1964 to 2016 using three key approaches. First, it preserved endangered art forms by hosting exhibitions featuring studio art and traditional techniques. The tradition of artists working together in studios has long been threatened by the ever-modernizing art world, yet it remains essential to the practice of printmaking, ceramics, glass, and many other art forms. The gallery showcased the important work done by remaining studios in the U.S. and the techniques which they maintained and created.

Second, the gallery celebrated Louisiana identity by featuring Louisiana culture and artists for exhibitions. The Union Art Gallery brought in many Louisiana artists and presented many events showcasing Louisiana culture and tradition. It also worked to feature artists and figures who have been influential in Louisiana history and who possess a unique understanding of it because of their lived experience.

Lastly, the gallery fostered critical dialogue with exhibitions addressing the struggles of Katrina, race relations in the 1940s, women’s history and more. Through these thought-provoking exhibitions, the Union Art Gallery established itself as more than just a display space, it became a forum for meaningful conversation and social engagement that enriched the entire LSU community.
